findings.source_passage: Tommy shook his head with a deep and somewhat overacted melancholy. 'I didn't want to disappoint you, old thing, by telling you right off. It's too bad. Good money wasted.'
findings.source_locator: Early exchange at the National Gallery, before Tommy reveals the two answers
findings.why_it_matters: The source has Tommy's 'deep and somewhat overacted melancholy' — a comic performance detail that establishes both his playfulness and the banter's theatrical quality. The draft drops 'overacted melancholy' and 'old thing,' flattening the voice-establishing comic register of the scene.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'deep and somewhat overacted melancholy' and the 'old thing' address; these are the specific comic markers Christie uses to establish the Tuppence-Tommy dynamic.

findings.source_passage: 'Ha!' said Tommy. 'Do I smell a Boche? Or only an American millionaire of unfortunate ancestry?'
findings.source_locator: After Tuppence reads the Hersheimmer letter
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves the line, which is good. However it cuts Tommy's follow-up reasoning about lunch ('a good time—frequently leads to free food for two') — this is present in the draft, so no loss there. No issue.
findings.suggested_fix: No action needed — line is preserved.

findings.source_passage: There was something very magnetic about Mr. Carter's personality. Tuppence seemed to shake herself free of it with an effort
findings.source_locator: After Carter's repeated 'Suppose you tell me...' and before Tuppence resists
findings.why_it_matters: This narratorial aside establishes Carter's characterisation as a man of unusual magnetic authority — a key interpretive detail for understanding why Tuppence, who is notably self-possessed, falters. The draft simply shows her resisting without explaining the psychological dynamic.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence about Carter's magnetic personality and Tuppence shaking herself free 'with an effort'; it is an interpretive-weight passage about character dynamics.

findings.source_passage: He was pro-German, as he would have been pro-Boer. What he seeks to attain we do not know--probably supreme power for himself, of a kind unique in history. We have no clue as to his real personality.
findings.source_locator: Carter's Mr. Brown speech, after 'On the contrary, I believe he is an Englishman'
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is interpretively significant: it establishes Mr. Brown as an ideological opportunist rather than a true partisan — 'pro-German as he would have been pro-Boer' — and plants the seed of 'supreme power for himself, of a kind unique in history.' This framing is essential to the novel's portrait of the master villain and is entirely absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: 'He was pro-German, as he would have been pro-Boer. What he seeks to attain we do not know—probably supreme power for himself, of a kind unique in history.' These are interpretive-weight lines for the Mr. Brown arc.

findings.source_passage: It was reported that even his own followers are ignorant of it. Where we have come across his tracks, he has always played a secondary part. Somebody else assumes the chief rôle.
findings.source_locator: Carter's Mr. Brown exposition, after 'We have no clue as to his real personality'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft collapses this into a single sentence and loses 'It was reported that even his own followers are ignorant of it' — a distinctive, chilling detail that matters for the novel's central mystery. The followers-don't-know detail is an interpretive keystone for how Mr. Brown operates.
findings.suggested_fix: Add back: 'It was reported that even his own followers are ignorant of it.' This specific fact is load-bearing for readers tracking the Mr. Brown mystery.

findings.source_passage: Now and then he passed his hand across his lips as though to hide a smile.
findings.why_it_matters: A small but characteristic physical detail that reveals Carter's barely concealed amusement at the Young Adventurers — part of Christie's gentle comedy of the establishment being charmed by these youngsters. Its absence removes a nuance of Carter's characterisation.
findings.suggested_fix: Add back the gesture of Carter passing his hand across his lips to hide a smile during Tuppence's account.

summary: The draft preserves the plot faithfully but erases four medium-severity voice and interpretive passages: Carter's magnetic-personality characterisation, the critical 'pro-German as he would have been pro-Boer / supreme power for himself' lines defining Mr. Brown's nature, the detail that even Brown's own followers don't know his identity, and Tommy's 'overacted melancholy' comic register — collectively triggering regeneration.
